That's also when everyone else's system fails, so calls pile up and waiting gets expensive. You're sitting in a house that gets warmer by the hour.

sections.heading: AC Repair
body: Most calls start the same way. The thermostat says 74, the house says 85, and the vents are blowing warm air. Or the outdoor unit hums and the fan never turns.

The cause is usually one small part: a capacitor that can't start the motor, a tired fan motor, a drain line clogged with algae. Heat wears all of them out, which is why they quit on the worst days. A repair that swaps one part costs far less than a new system.
We find what failed, show you what it is and get the cold air back.

If it's time, we install energy-efficient air conditioning systems matched to your home. Financing is available through Enhancify, so a replacement doesn't have to land all at once.

sections.heading: What Usually Fails, and Why
body: Air conditioners fail in the heat because heat is when they work hardest. Here is what fails most often:
list: **Capacitors.** A small part that gives the motors the jolt to start. It weakens with heat and age, then the fan or compressor won't start. It is one of the cheapest and most common failures.
**Fan and compressor motors.** Hours of Kansas heat wear bearings and windings until the motor stalls or quits.
**Low refrigerant.** A system doesn't use up refrigerant, so low levels mean a leak somewhere that needs finding, not just topping off.
**Clogged drain line.** Algae blocks the condensate drain and a safety switch shuts the system down.
**Frozen coil.** Restricted airflow, usually from a dirty filter, lets the coil ice over and stops cooling.
tail: A technician who finds the real cause fixes it once. One who guesses sends you a second bill.

sections.heading: Repair or Replace?
body: A repair is usually the right call when the system is fairly young and one part has failed. A new capacitor or motor on a system that otherwise runs well is money well spent.
Replacement starts to make sense when the system is old, keeps breaking, or can't keep the house cool even when every part works. Spending repeatedly on a system near the end of its life rarely pays.

We give you the numbers on both and let you choose. If you go with a new system, financing is available through Enhancify. Our [AC replacement page](/ac-replacement-wichita-ks/) explains what to expect.

sections.heading: Not Sure It's the AC?
body: Before you call, a quick check can save you a visit:
list: Confirm the thermostat is set to cool, below the room temperature, with working batteries.
Check that the breaker for the outdoor unit and the indoor air handler hasn't tripped.
Look at your air filter. If it's packed with dust, replace it.
Check for ice on the refrigerant lines or the indoor coil. If you see ice, turn the system off and let it thaw before calling.
tail: If those don't fix it, give us a call. Tell us what you see and hear, and that helps us arrive with the right parts.

sections.heading: When the System Is Telling You It's Done
body: You've paid for the same system three summers running. It runs all afternoon and the house still sits at 82. The outdoor unit rattles, the vents are weak, or the electric bill climbs while the comfort drops.
None of those alone means replace. Together they usually do. A system that keeps failing has parts wearing out one after another, and each repair buys a few months, not years.

sections.heading: Why Old Systems Cost More Every Year
body: Most central air conditioners are built to last somewhere around 10 to 15 years. Kansas summers sit at the hard end of that range, because the system runs for months at a stretch.
As a system ages, three things happen.

Parts wear out faster, so repair calls come closer together. It uses more electricity to deliver less cooling, because the motors and coils are worn and efficiency standards were lower when it was built. And a system that uses the older R-22 refrigerant is getting costly to service, because that refrigerant is no longer produced.
A new system fixes all three at once.

sections.heading: Repair First, When Repair Makes Sense
body: Replacement is not where we start. A young system with one failed part should be repaired, and we'll tell you so.

When we come out, the technician finds what failed and explains your options in plain words: repair the part, replace a major component, or replace the system. You get the reasoning and the numbers on each, and you decide.
We're a new company, and our reputation rests on advice like this. If your system has years left, you'll hear that from us.

sections.heading: What We Install
body: We install energy-efficient air conditioning systems for homes, matched to your house and your needs. The goal is a system that is the right size for your home, not the biggest one on the truck.

Size matters more than most people expect. A system that is too large cools the air quickly, shuts off and never pulls much moisture out, so the house feels clammy. One that is too small runs without stopping and still can't keep up on a 100-degree day.
If your furnace is also near the end of its life, we install and replace furnaces too. Replacing both together means the two pieces of equipment are matched.

list: What equipment is being installed, and its efficiency rating
What's included in the install, and what the old system's removal covers
Whether your existing ductwork and thermostat are staying or changing
Who stands behind the work after the crew leaves
tail: If a quote leaves those out, you're comparing a number, not a system. Ask us for each of them at your free estimate.
